utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning to you all. There's a matter the Chamber wanted to raise in the absence of the witness. Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now in open session. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Suljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, as yesterday, I'm going to ask you to be as concise as possible in your comments. We're just going to pick up where we left off yesterday. And the first document, if I could have 10932, please. Mr. Suljevic, as you'll see, this is a document issued by the SRK Command on the 24th of August, 1995, once it's on your screen. If you could just tell us what that document is about.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is an order to issue aerial bombs to various units. It is the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps that compiled the document, and then it says how many aerial bombs are going to be issued to each and every brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones be switched off while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have the next document, which is 11643, please. It's a fairly short document, Mr. Suljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, if you could just describe what this one is.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document also shows that the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is urgently asking the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to allow them to issue aerial bombs in order to crush the Muslim offensive; namely, 30 105-kilogram bombs and 20 250-kilogram bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have the next document, please, which is 11647.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Again, it's a fairly short document, Mr. Suljevic. Just tell us who it's from and to and what it's about.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Technical Department, that is writing and saying that the 27th Logistics Brigade will take over the aerial bomb from the Pretis company once they are completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have the next document, which is 11804.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This appears to be a request, as you can see, Mr. Suljevic, in relation to various kinds of ammunition. If you could tell us, just briefly, what kinds of ammunition are being requested, and then focus on items 15 and 16.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is addressing the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, asking them to equip units that are involved in intensive combat activity. On the list, there is artillery ammunition from 76- to 150-millimetre calibre, then mortar shells for mortars, 82-millimetre and 120-millimetre, and, finally, inter alia, the issuing of aerial bombs, 20 105-kilogram bombs and 10 250-kilogram bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have the next document, which is 11815.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And this document, Mr. Suljevic, if you could focus on items 7, 8, and 9 under Section B, and tell us what the document is.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's similar to the previous one. The Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is addressing the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and is most urgently asking for the issuing of ammunition needed for potential anti-landing combat; inter alia, it has to do with the issuing of 105-kilogram aerial bombs and 250-kilogram aerial bombs and 128-millimetre rockets, known as Plamen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have the next document, which is 11816.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Suljevic, you might want to cast your eye to the middle of the section marked "Section 2." And, again, just generally describe what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just zoom out a bit so that I can see it better, so that I see the beginning? This is information concerning the receipt of material and financial resources, and it says that in 1995, equipment was received according to this list; inter alia, a certain number of aerial bombs of 100 kilograms and a certain number of 250-kilogram bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can we have the next document, please, which is 11817.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And, Mr. Suljevic, this document, could you just say who it's from, who it's to, and then look at item 22 under Section A.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document shows that it was sent from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. This document is a request for approval concerning ammunition in order to equip units that are engaged in intensive combat operations. Ten 250-kilogram bombs are requested, inter alia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you just clarify what kind of 250-kilogram bombs are requested?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Air-bombs, aerial bombs that are mentioned in all the documents that we had here, that we saw yesterday, that were used for construction -- actually, for constructing modified air-bombs, those that consisted of an air-bomb and an engine as a launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have the next document, which is 11818.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is a document, as you can see, Mr. Suljevic, from the VRS Main Staff to be delivered to Pretis and to the SRK Command. And if you could tell us what it's about, and, again, just identify items 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This shows that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, or, rather, the Technical Department in the Logistics Sector, is writing to the Pretis company. They're ordering them, actually, or asking them to issue a certain type of ammunition. Inter alia, they're asking for FAB-100 bombs, three of them; FAB-250 bombs, three of them. I think that these are modified air-bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have the next document, please, which is 11819.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Again, just tell us what this document is. It appears to be issued by the VRS Main Staff. Tell us, briefly, what it's about.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Like previously, the Technical Department of the Logistics Sector of the VRS is sending a document to the Command of the 27th Logistics Brigade and the Pretis company. This is a document that says the following: "Upon the request of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command (for units on the north-western part of the Sarajevo front), the following types and quantities of ammunition are to be issued and transported to the village of Semizovac:" Inter alia, an FAB-250/3 air-bomb is requested; actually, four of them. I think they're actually asking for four modified air-bombs. That's in the first part. As for meeting the needs of the units at the south-western part of the front, a certain type of ammunition should be sent to Lukavica as well. Inter alia, an FAB-105 air-bomb is requested, five of them, actually, and an FAB 250, three of them. I think that what is requested are those modified air-bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, as we can see, one of the references you've pointed out, in fact, reads "FAB BA 105." Would you care to comment as to what that might be?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what that means, exactly. I assume that it may be a typo. Instead of typing a hyphen, somebody typed out "BA." That's my opinion. I think it is air-bombs that are marked "FAB-105."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have the next document, which is 12123.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document is from the SRK Command, and it's headed "Talas-1" at the top right-hand corner. This is quite a long document, Mr. Suljevic. If you could describe what it appears to be to you. And then if we could go to page 2 and focus on the first three paragraphs on page 2 after you've had an opportunity to look at the first page.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we have a look at page 2? There is a page 2, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. If you could focus, in fact, on the very top of page 2, the first three typewritten paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document shows that within this operation, an order was issued to prepare launchers and to select a target for launching four to six aerial bombs, provided that they hit the target. This document shows that if that many bombs do not fall on that particular target, more bombs should be used. So if they miss, the next projectile has to hit the target. It also says that what should be envisaged is using aerial bombs against three more designated targets in addition to the main target, and that at least two projectiles should fall on those targets; that is to say, two air bombs, at least. In terms of the preparation of all of this equipment, Colonel Tadija Manojlovic is tasked with this particular assignment, and these air-bombs should be used in given areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just going back to the last few words of the first paragraph on that page, do you have any observations to make on what you have read there?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, it says that if a target is missed, it should be made sure that the next projectile has to hit the target. That is to say, if the launched aerial bomb does not hit the target, then, as far as I understand this document, it has to be made sure that the target will be hit as many times as necessary before it is actually hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. And just as a general matter, could you summarise what this document is, to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please have the first page. This is an order to act, as the document, itself, says, within the context of preparing for Talas-1; that is, an action that is called Talas-1. This is an order of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command, issued to the units that are listed here in the document. These are probably units that belonged to that corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have the next document, please, which is 15891.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, this has been admitted as Exhibit D322.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could move to the second page on the B/C/S version of this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Again, could you describe, briefly, what this document is, and then focus on the words which appear to be underlined in the version which you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is issuing a very urgent order related to full combat readiness for all units of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. The document shows that there is information to the effect that the enemy is planning operations against the units of the corps. In order to thwart that, what is being ordered, inter alia, is what we can see from part of the text; namely, to ensure that launchers and air-bombs should be prepared to fire on the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have the next document, please, 20841.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next document, Mr. Suljevic, as you'll see, is a document from the SRK Command to the VRS Main Staff. Can you tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is sending to the Main Staff of the VRS a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps we can zoom in on the text a little.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is a report of the chief of artillery of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to the VRS Main Staff, where he's informing the Main Staff that he was unable and that he gave up on targeting the designated target, which envisaged, according to the decision that had been made, to target the entrance to the tunnel in Donji Kotorac. They decided to desist from that because their own forces and the UN forces would thus be placed in jeopardy. And as we can see from the document, during the reconnaissance that was carried out in preparation for carrying out this task, it was established that there were two UNPROFOR check-points some 200 metres, at most, from the entrance to the tunnel, and that the UNPROFOR observers were moving around in the town of Kotorac from their check-points, and that some VRS position was some 500 metres away from the entrance to the tunnel, and that the direction of the targeting would be over the Restaurant Kula, which was -- as we can see, the target was, in my view, on the other side of the airport. And to me this looks like a document that shows how imprecise this system of launching aerial bombs was, because if they are afraid that they might strike their own units, which are very far from the designated target, that points to a conclusion that the chief of artillery, himself, was not certain about where this air-bomb might actually strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have the next document, please, which is 20850.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: As you'll see, Mr. Suljevic, this is a request from the Ilidza PBR Command to the SRK Command, dated the 10th of the 6th, 1995. Just look down at paragraph two and just summarise what this document's about.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Command of the 1st Ilidza Brigade is requesting from the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to provide them assets or means, as it says in the document, for the production of 250-kilogram air-bombs. And for the 30 pieces -- or, rather, 30 sets of -- in my view, of these modified air-bombs, they requested motors, because they didn't have them, and that's what they're requesting in this document addressed to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. So they are requesting to be provided 90 motors for modified air-bombs, 250-kilogram air-bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Does that fit in with your understanding of how many engines were attached to a 250-kilogram air-bomb?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is consistent with that, although in the investigations that I participated in, we also found air-bombs that would have four rocket motors fitted on them. There were some that had three. And, of course, I'm only speaking about the investigations that I participated in. Here, if we have 30 air-bombs, and the request is for 90 rocket motors, then, based on this, it would appear that these 30 air-bombs would be fitted with three rocket motors each.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have the next document, please, which is 20852.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: As you'll see in a moment, Mr. Suljevic, this is a document from the Vogosca IKM of the SRK Command, addressed to the VRS Main Staff. And if you can confirm that and also look at paragraph 6 of this document.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see from this document that there was an offensive which was repelled, all the attacks were repelled successfully, and then further on it says that the 27th Logistics Base had taken over a certain quantity of ammunition from the Pretis enterprise, more specifically, 120-millimetre shells and 105-millimetre rounds, and that there were some more -- there were further quantities that could be taken over from the Pretis enterprise. And it further says that there were aerial bombs that should be collected, FAB-100 and FAB-250; in total, 29 pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have the next document, please, which is 20853.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is a document, Mr. Suljevic, as you can see, from the Forward Command Post of the SRK Command to the SRK commander. And tell us what this is about.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document shows that this was -- this is a proposal, and I think that we had a similar document -- that we saw a similar document yesterday, where the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command is being informed that the Maintenance and Repair Depot in Hadzici has manufactured a new air-bomb launcher for up to 500-kilogram bombs. And as it says in the document, it is of much higher quality than any so far. The launcher is mounted on a vehicle taken from the Igman Brigade, and that the technical control was tested at the Maintenance and Repair Depot, but that there should be a commission established - or, rather, that's the proposal - in order to establish the consumption of FABs, 100 and 250 kilograms, and that following the testing that it should be deployed with one of the corps artillery units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I have the next document, please, which is 20855.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you tell us, generally, what this document is, and then focus on items 6 and 7 on the first part and also items 6 and 7 in the other two parts of this document.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a request for ammunition replenishment, sent to the chief of artillery of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, where, in the first part, they are presenting the ammunition that they have available within units. And according to this document, the status of ammunition at a certain location is -- and then it mentions the air-bomb, 250, it says, "KT," and a 250-kilogram air-bomb, and that they don't have them at this particular position, whereas in the second paragraph we see that at another position, Position RR, they do have one air-bomb of 250 kilograms and three 100-kilogram air bombs. That is the status and the situation. And then what follows is a request to replenish the ordnance. Could we see -- could we scroll down and see the text further.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's on the next page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, as I've already said, the first part shows the status and the situation as it is, a snap-shot of what they have, whereas the second part is a request where they are requesting five 250-kilogram air-bombs and three 100-kilogram air-bombs, which is consistent with what it says there; that for the 100-kilogram air-bomb, they need 1.5 combat sets, whereas for the five 250-kilogram air-bombs, 2.5 combat sets are required.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have the next document, please, which is 20857.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we zoom in on that document, Mr. Suljevic, no need to worry about the handwritten annotations. Just tell us who it's from, and who it's to, and what this concerns.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the fifth line from the bottom in this text, there is mention of 500-kilogram bombs. I don't know if this is an error of some sort. So this is a request for 250-kilogram bombs, which corresponds to the 2.5 combat sets, and then 100-kilogram bombs for which they're requesting 1.5 combat sets, which we saw in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just focus on the opening paragraphs of the communication. Perhaps we can zoom in a little on the text of the opening paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is asking the subordinate units, as far as I can see, to return a certain number of air-bombs, pursuant to a verbal order by General Miletic, from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, that these air-bombs which had been captured from Pretis by the 3rd Brigade when they attacked the factory, and that were deployed according to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps pursuant to an order of the 24th of August, 1995, and apparently this deployment was made in error because, as it says in the Command from the IKM 2, the recovered ammunition should be distributed to various units. And then further on, it says that in relation to the -- that the -- to the above-mentioned matter, it is necessary that the units in the north-west section of the Sarajevo theatre return the air-bombs to Pretis. And then they mention that there are 105 and 250-kilogram bombs that need to be returned. The total number of the bombs to be returned are 12 105-kilogram bombs and 14 250-kilogram bombs. And once the task is accomplished, they should report to the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're on to the final document, which is 21325. And if we could zoom in on the text a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And tell us who this is from, who it is to, and what this document is.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, sent to the Pretis holding company in Vogosca and to the command of some units -- commands of some units. The order says that for the needs of HK units engaged in Zvijezda operation plus 94. On the right bank of the Drina River, they should issue seven prepared FAB 250-kilogram air-bombs, and for the needs of the units, to also issue seven prepared 250-kilogram air bombs. But it says that the launcher -- the use of launchers and air bombs will be only in co-ordination with the Command of the Visegrad Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And could you give the full name of that unit, if you can? Or, essentially, I just wanted, as much as you can tell, what the last few words of the body of the communications state.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says in the document that the use of the launcher and the 250-kilogram air-bombs will be carried out in agreement with the commander of the DK and the Visegrad TG. I think that the Visegrad "TG" means "Tactical Group," and the "DK" is probably a corps, a reference to a corps. At least that's what it says, but I'm not sure -- I'm not very familiar with all of these units, nor am I familiar with the composition of the corps and their units and what units were in which corps. I am not familiar, either, with the composition of the Bosnian Army or the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At this stage, Mr. President, I'd like to seek the admission of the 45 documents that the witness has commented upon. And I'd also like to seek the admission of the documents listed in his amalgamated witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I note that four of these documents were admitted as source documents from Mr. Philipps' testimony. I don't know if you need me to list them, or probably Ram already has that information. But if it's necessary, I can give you the 65 ter numbers and the P numbers. Apart from that, although there may be grounds for objecting to some of these documents through this witness, in the spirit of reciprocity and anticipated reciprocity in the future, we don't object. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In respect of the documents which have been admitted as source documents previously, we're now seeking the admission of those documents for all purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering the associated exhibits at this moment as well, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'll tender all the associated exhibits referred to in the amalgamated witness statement. While I'm at it: Your Honours requested us to take a hard look at the associated exhibits which concern unscheduled shelling incidents. You made an oral direction to that effect. I've done that, and all but one of the unscheduled shelling incidents are supported by one document each. In each case, the document is a two- or three-page KDZ report. And in respect of one unscheduled shelling incident, it's supported by two documents. So we could -- if you wish, we could remove 09924 from the list of documents referred to in the list which appears at the end of the amalgamated statement of Mr. Suljevic. It's attached to the very end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you have any observation as to the associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't object to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, in relation to 65 ter 9719 -- or, no, strike that. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be all admitted. And those four items which were admitted through Mr. Philipps as source documents, they will be noted as having been admitted for full purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That ends the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Good morning, Mr. Suljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Cross-examination by Karadzic:

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I will not be able to deal with any general issues. However, I would like to clarify one point. In your folder, I received a document of which I'm not sure whether it belongs there. Let me ask you: Did you actually participate in the war, in our war?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify? What do you mean when you say "participate in the war"? I was, from before the war, an employee of the Zrak special-purpose company up to sometime in late 1993, and then I joined the Republican Ministry of the Internal Affairs. It's the Department for Counter-Sabotage. And while I was there, and I'm still there - only now it is a federal institution - I was tasked with different duties. But my department was not a combat unit, and it never participated in any combat. I was never on any front-lines, I was never among BiH Army members.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you produce before 1993, when you were still working at the Zrak company?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm an engineer, a machine engineer, and I was -- I'm a mechanical engineer, and I was involved in the construction of devices and machinery for special-purpose industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If your CV is correct, then I would say you were involved in the production of optical sights.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Zrak company, as you know, is a company that deals with mechanical and optical devices. I was engaged in the construction of optical and electronic devices. More specifically, those were devices and mechanisms for the navigation of rockets, for semi-automatic rocket guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: But you are a mechanical engineer, not an electrical engineer?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a mechanical engineer, and my specialty is production of mechanical devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Then, in that case, I've received a folder belonging to some other Suljevic. Do you know somebody called Suljevic who was affiliated with the Administration for Strategic Planning and Education of Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I heard of General Zico Suljevic. I never met him, though, and I don't know where he is from. I don't know of any other people by the name of Suljevic. I don't know a single person who was affiliated with the army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please show this signature to the witness. I would like to be sure whether this, indeed, is his document or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the usher could show the document to the Prosecutor first, and then show it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I received this only at the very last moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The problem's solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's fine. We don't have to see them?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the signature is not his, then no. The OTP has erroneously and unintentionally included that document with all the others that do belong to this witness's portfolio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, could you please tell us which aerial bombs existed? Could you tell us their weight? What kind of aerial bombs existed in the former Yugoslavia, in terms of their weight and charges?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the former Yugoslav Army had, which aerial bombs they had at their disposal before the war. And during the war, in the incidents -- or, rather, in the investigations that I was involved in, I had an occasion to see -- or, rather, those were -- that was not an investigation. It was just an inspection of a location above Bascarsija, where we found an aerial bomb that had not exploded. We found it in the canyon of the river. Its body was cracked, it's shell was cracked, and it was a 250-kilogram aerial bomb. During the reintegration of the Sarajevo municipalities after the war, I saw photos depicting 250-kilogram aerial bombs. Some of my colleagues had seen them in the Ilijas Ironworks. I, myself, am not an expert. While I served in the former army, I was not affiliated with any such units that would provide me with any knowledge. All I know is from literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. What do you mean when you say "the reintegration of Sarajevo municipalities"? Do you mean the taking over of Serbian municipalities which belonged to the federation after the Dayton Accords, Ilijas, Vogosca, the Serbian part of Vogosca, and others?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the process of reintegration. That's the official term. After the Dayton Accords, you call it taking over, but that means that according to the Dayton Agreement, some municipalities were given to the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you confuse me a little. Does that mean that you came in touch with aerial bombs only during the last war in 1994 or 1995, not before?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In the course of the war, I came into a position to acquire knowledge and information about all sorts of artillery projectiles. Before the war, I had not undergone any artillery training, not even in -- while serving in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. When was the first time you encountered aerial bombs in the last war? I'm specifically referring to aerial bombs and their impact and characteristics.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a specific date. I believe that one of the first -- or the first aerial bomb exploded, and I subsequently investigated that place, and that was an aerial bomb which fell by the Sarajka Department Store, next to the Institute for Pulmonary Diseases, in Stevo Street, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And before that, you had not received any instruction in that sense?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, then let me ask you a few questions and see whether we can agree on some things. In addition to the 105- and 250-kilogram aerial bombs -- do the kilograms actually denote the explosives, the quantity of the explosives in those bombs?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you what I know. I'm not an expert, and I do not appear here in the role of an expert. The kilograms do not denote the quantity of explosives. I believe that this is the actual weight of the aerial bomb, the order of magnitude. As far as I can remember, the 250-kilogram aerial bomb actually contains about 100 kilo of explosives. At least that's what I read in literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Am I right in saying that in addition to those two, there were also 500-kilo, 1.000-kilo, and 2.000-kilo aerial bombs as well?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say, I can't answer. I am sure that probably -- or, rather, I'm sure that there was a 500-kilogram bomb. Whether the former army had the other two, 1.000-kilo and 2.000-kilo, I don't know. I suppose that there are bombs of that sort worldwide.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Suljevic. And now could you please tell us, according to your information, what could have been the descent speed of those bombs, or, rather, impact velocity, in metres per second or kilometres per hour?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you that information. I'm not privy to that information at all. We never determined velocity of any of the projectiles at their place of impact. I suppose it cannot be determined. I suppose, for the artillery ammunition, you have to start from the launch velocity to the impact velocity, and the distance, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that while you were studying or investigating the place of the air-bomb incident, did you take into account the fragments that you found there and did you take into account the effects of the bomb, the effects that that bomb produced, and that based on that, inter alia, based on that, you arrived at your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, if you don't know enough about those bombs, you don't know their impact velocity, you don't know their weights, types, and so on and so forth, how did you manage to cope without the necessary information and knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when it comes to aerial bombs, or an aerial bomb which was most probably used in most of my reports, or, rather, that my reports refer to, and that's the 250-kilo aerial bomb, there is a lot of information in literature. There is its diametre, for example. And at the air-bomb incident places, we always came across the adapter or the bore that connected the aerial bomb and the motors. And based on the diametre of that plate, we were able to claim that it was, indeed, a bomb that we thought it was, because this particular aerial bomb, if I can remember well, its diametre is about 400 millimetres. I'm talking about the 250-kilogram aerial bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the largest or the biggest fragment that you ever encountered? What was the biggest piece of shrapnel that you ever recovered at the place of an air-bomb incident?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak off the top of my head without my reports, but I can say that one of the biggest aerial bomb shrapnel was a piece of tin or a piece of iron when one of the aerial bombs fell very close to the house where I resided in a meadow which was about 200 metres away from my house. A big shrapnel, a big piece of iron, possibly about 10 millimetres thick, and approximately 10-by-20 centimetres big, and that shrapnel actually ended up on the roof of my house. And we found the types of shrapnel that were described in our reports. I can't remember their dimensions, but I don't think that we ever found anything as big as that in any other places --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you participate in the investigation of that particular incident which took place 200 metres away from your house?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't know whether there was an investigation at all, because there were -- there were no casualties. It was a weekend, probably, because I was at home. It was in the summer. The weather was nice. There were no casualties. There was a lot of material damage on the facilities. Nothing was destroyed, because there were no houses close to the place of impact. But, for example, on my house, all the window-panes were shattered, all the glass was shattered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the meadow that you're talking about, was it a soft surface?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a meadow. It was a grassy surface, soft, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: But did you see the crater? How big was the crater? Could you describe it?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did come close to the crater, to the place of the air-bomb incident, and in the place I also found representatives of the UNPROFOR or whatever units were on the ground at the time. I don't know. That crater was in the meadow, and its size was three by two, and its depth was about a metre and a half. I don't know. I'm speaking from memory. Nobody measured it at the time, so it's very hard for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you agree with me -- or, rather, did you hear that those bigger aerial bombs, 250 kilos, 1.000 kilos, and 2.000 kilos, that they have a popular name? How are they known, popularly?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they call them "krmaca." I don't know whether they were all known as "krmaca" or "sow." I don't know whether it was just one or all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that "krmaca" is actually a female pig?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you agree that people called them that because they are fat, big, and messy, and they -- wherever they fall, they cause a lot of mess?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, aerial bombs are intended for destruction. That's their purpose, to destroy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. What's the time of combustion of those motors that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't give you that information. We were never asked to present that in our report, so I never came across information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And do you agree -- or, rather, does it sound familiar to you that the combustion time of those rockets is four seconds? You spoke about that yesterday. You told us that the combustion time is from the time of launching to the target. Will you agree with me that the combustion time of those rockets is four minutes? No, no, I apologise, four seconds, four seconds.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already that I don't know about that, but it is only natural that a projectile will not fall automatically once the fuel has all burned. There is going to be inertia. It will go on flying, won't it, and then it will fall where it falls.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, did you confuse me yesterday when you said that fuel is used to propel a rocket -- or, no, not a rocket, a bomb to its target.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps this was lack of precision. Well, I don't know what was fired, but if it's four seconds, as you said, then if it takes it four seconds to get there, but if the flight is longer than that, the projectile will still go on flying because there is inertia. It will fly until it falls on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask for page references, if the accused is referring to yesterday's testimony of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you identify the page number, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll get that during the course of the examination. We'll get that ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Suljevic, do you agree that these rockets, these rocket engines, also have their own mathematics? There are tables that are used to set the target?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree. As to their purpose, I have no doubts that all the necessary tests were carried out. Now, as far as tests are concerned and military checks, I am familiar with that to the extent to which we tested various devices. So I don't doubt that those rockets had been tested and that tables were worked out for them, but only for their basic purpose; that is to say, to fire rockets that had these warheads, if I can put it that way, and that were fired from multiple rocket-launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. But do you know or do you have proof -- since we're talking about mathematics, the quantity of fuel, then time, and so on and so forth, do you have information to the effect that this could not have been done, regardless of what these rocket engines are carrying; one, two, three, or more?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not understand your question. Could you be a bit more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You confirmed, when speaking of Grad rockets, that you believe that very precise elements were calculated for the firing of this rocket. Now, do you have any information or proof or do you believe that it is impossible to attain that, regardless of how many engines there are and what kind of warheads are going to be involved? Do you agree that this is a question of mathematics?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that this is a question of mathematics and making the right calculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, this is the second time this happened. The accused's reference to Mr. Suljevic's testimony concerning the Grad rockets does not agree with the transcript I have, nor does it agree with the amalgamated statement of the witness. So I simply ask, if he wishes to refer to the evidence of Mr. Suljevic, either point us to a paragraph in his amalgamated statement or to a page of yesterday's transcript, and that would make it much easier to understand what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are referring to his statement that the witness confirmed, when speaking of Grad rockets, that he --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the witness believes that very precise elements were calculated?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: For firing of this rocket, that's right. And earlier on, the accused referred to a statement by the witness that fuel was used to propel a particular kind of projectile, and I do not recall Mr. Suljevic saying that in his evidence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. Could you give us the reference, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was referring to what Mr. Suljevic stated yesterday; namely, that a rocket is propelled from its point of firing to its target. What I put to Mr. Suljevic today was that the burning goes on for four seconds, and after that he spoke of inertia and so on. However, today, on page 26, I think, Mr. Suljevic confirmed that these rockets have certain elements that had been calculated, and a great deal of precision, too, and he restricted himself to the warheads that they were designed for. That's what happened today. And then I asked him whether he agreed that it was a question of calculating fuel, precision, et cetera, that was a question of mathematics, and Mr. Suljevic agreed that it was a question of mathematics. And I asked Mr. Suljevic whether he had any proof that that was impossible to attain if the warhead is different or if two, three, or four engines are used for something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What you paraphrased is a bit different from what he originally said. In any event, the witness answered. But in the future, be precise in paraphrasing or referring to his earlier statement. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic. One more question and we'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wouldn't be paraphrasing if the learned Mr. Gaynor had been following what Mr. Suljevic had been saying in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you confirmed, Mr. Suljevic, this is a question of mathematics. Do you have any proof to the effect that it is not possible to calculate precision, or, rather, the firing elements if one applies mathematics to other magnitudes?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When applying mathematics and carrying out all tests - in the army and in the army industry, people know about that - the technical requirements of a particular piece of equipment that is being manufactured involves this, so all of these requirements have to be tested. And after that, appropriate tables are issued, instructions, and so on and so forth. That is a generally-known thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would this be the right time for a break, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if it is convenient. We'll have a break for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, I'm afraid that I omitted to establish the time with you. You kindly referred to the place where you first encountered an air-bomb. Could you tell us the approximate month and year?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say what the month or the year was. I think that we saw it at some later point. We don't know exactly when it fell. Now, was that the end of 1994, was it 1995? I really don't know when it happened, but it was certainly considerably after the bomb actually fell, because I do not have any information as to when this bomb was first noticed, let alone when it was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We are talking about the crater on the meadow near your house. Are you sure it was an air-bomb?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that you were asking me about the first unexploded bomb I had seen, and that is what my answer pertained to. As for this other bomb, I'm sure that it was a modified air-bomb because there were four rocket engines that were tied up there and they happened to be in the crater. I'm sure that it was an aerial bomb, an air-bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just tell us the time. When did that happen, approximately?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you it was summertime.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on to some of the cases that you worked on, can you tell us when does a projectile have regular dispersion and when does it have abnormal dispersion, and how is that established in the first place?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to repeat what I said. I am not testifying as an expert here, but I can give you my opinion. When projectiles are being examined -- or, rather, when any other equipment is being examined, the examinations are very, very precise. As far as I know from literature for artillery projectiles, and the tables that I had occasion to see and read, these examinations take a long time. As far as projectiles are concerned, when firing tables are being elaborated, mathematics involves a great many factors; say, altitude, ballistic characteristics, the meteorological conditions involved. As I've already said, all equipment has to be examined. It is not clear to me what kind of examination had taken place. Yesterday, we had a document where one air-bomb of 100 kilograms or of 250 kilograms is supposed to be tested -- or, rather, the launcher for 500 kilograms is being tested. I don't think you even test a bicycle that way. You don't test it with a child that weighs 50 kilograms and then say that the bicycle can carry a 100-kilogram person, a man who weighs 100 kilograms. So this could not be relevant, especially as far as this specific case is concerned, to conduct the testing of a launcher for an air-bomb in this one particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is determined by way of a formula, which is 3 VV times 3 WP?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exclude that possibility, but I never worked on determining ballistic characteristics. I don't rule that out, but as I said, you have to take into account all factors. These tests have to take into account all factors in order to have precise firing tables. Of course, after that there is the probability of dispersion. So there are no tables that can make sure that a target is hit with 100 per cent certainty. There is always this dispersion that has to be allowed for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Excellent. That's what you said. 3 VV times 3 VP, is that the criterion of precision?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember that UNPROFOR asked the Muslim artillery and mortar crews to move their positions at least 500 metres away from UNPROFOR positions and installations so that they would not be affected by retaliatory fire?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what do you say to this: Are rocket projectiles more precise or are artillery projectiles more precise?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. As far as I know, I never worked on the elaboration of tables and I never carried out comparisons, so I cannot give a precise answer to your question. But I know that there is always the probability of hitting the target that exists in all tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, but didn't you have to know about that, because you were dealing with the points of impact where artillery and rocket and mortar shells fell; right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. We worked on investigations at points of impact in order to determine what the type of projectile was and also to see what the trajectory was. That's what I worked on. We did not know and we could not even guess what it was that they were trying to hit, what the marksman was trying to hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, how did you make a distinction between artillery and mortar projectiles?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, that was discussed a bit. We looked at the traces that were found on site. On the basis of certain characteristic designations or traces on the shrapnel found, and on the basis of what this actually looked like, or, rather, what the crater looked like, or, rather, the traces around the crater that was created by the impact, the point of impact of a projectile that does not rotate is different. This is mortar projectiles, for instance. It's different from artillery projectiles that do rotate during their trajectory. That is to say, they rotate around their axis once they're fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So what is this difference? How can you tell at the point of impact?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mortar shells have characteristic traces. Well, they had a particular name. It was called the rosette and the paw of the crater. That is to say, it's around the point of impact, itself. It's a bit hard to explain this by using words. It consists of some circles, or an ellipsis, rather, around the crater. Well, the greater the concentration of shrapnel, I mean, on that side where the projectile had landed, as opposed to artillery projectiles, where the traces are not that characteristic, I mean, the traces that are left by the projectile as it falls.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you sketch this difference to show the Trial Chamber and the Defence -- to show what actually the crater looks like, where you can tell whether it is a mortal shell or an artillery shell? That would help us with examining -- or while examining and testing your findings here, and it will help us understand them more easily.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can try.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can do this during the break. Maybe Mr. Suljevic can use his break, or if he would be gracious enough to use part of his break, in order to draw a sketch of the point of impact in the instances of one and the other type of projectile, artillery or mortar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised that the witness is able to draw, drawing in the e-court in a blank page, if necessary, through e-court. He can do it right now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, if we can do it that way, then that's perfect. Could we have it, then, in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks] [Interpretation] As far as it was possible to do it here - it is rather clumsy - but approximately this is what an impact of a mortar shell would look like. In the center, we see the point of impact at the moment when the projectile is activated, and the dots around it are, in fact, the scrapings or the damage to the surface which was impacted, and these markings were created by the fragments of an exploding projectile. And, of course, this would depend on the angle at which the projectile hits the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, do you consider this to be an image of a mortar shell impact? And will you please note that down and put down the date and your name.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Would you now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 22nd of July, Mr. Suljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please now, on the other half of the screen, make a sketch of a trace or impact of an artillery shell and what it looks like?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we change the colour into blue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how successful I will be, but the traces are not similar. As far as I had occasion to see, around this central point, the point of impact of the projectile, the fragments would disperse and the damage on the surface that was impacted would spread and disperse approximately in this manner [marks]. And, of course, there are probably fragments there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you please again write down what this depicts and write your name and date?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll save this, and we'll admit it as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D525, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your statements at some point, and in your findings, you mentioned at some point high-explosive projectiles. Could you please describe what that means? What do you consider a highly explosive projectile?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you can show me the document where that is, because I cannot do it without it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, we will try to do that. But could you please tell me whether there is a difference between highly explosive projectiles and the contact or impact -- impact and contact projectiles?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contact-action projectiles are projectiles that have a dual possibility of action or effectiveness, the immediate-impact and also the contact-impact. But I believe it cannot really be projected.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you tell us now, please, what is the most common angle of incidence for a ricochet projectile in the case of air-bombs?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What would that depend on?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, this is something for experts to say. But in my view, that angle would depend on the fuse. And if the fuse is not activated at the point of impact, then there may be a ricochet action following after that. At least, that is my opinion, but I believe this is a question for an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. But will you agree with me that the angle of incidence and the outgoing angle in the case of a ricochet projectile, that they are related and they depend on each other?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would depend on the surface of -- where a projectile impacts. It would not always be the same instance. For instance, if a projectile lands at the same spot, the angle of incidence would depend on the hardness of the surface, because if it is not irrelevant whether the angle of descent of incidence is flat or the point of incidence is flat or at a certain angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: But will you agree with me that after a ricochet, the trajectory would actually go up; correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after a ricochet effect, that's what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the indictment against me, there is a scheduled incident of Safeta Hadzica Street. However, it is impossible to understand that incident without linking it to the incident of the BH RTV of 28th June, and what I would like to ask you now is whether you investigated this incident involving the television building.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not investigate the Safet Hadzic incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. But the TV incident, you investigated that; correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was one of the persons investigating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You concluded that the bomb actually hit the roof of the passage and that then it ricochetted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was established that the roof bore the signs of an impact. Now, whether this was a bomb that landed there or whether only the propulsion piece hit there, that was impossible to determine, especially because we were not able to find that at all, the fragments of that. It probably fell off somewhere in flight. And all I had was some information, although I've never seen it officially written down, that this propulsion element was later seen somewhere near the Miljetska River, but that is only something that I heard mentioned. I didn't really -- I wasn't really able to confirm that information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 65 ter 09851 in e-court. And as part of that document, I would like to see the image number 3. 09851, 09851; picture 3 of that document. The pages are 104-3352.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction: 3552.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, what can we see in the picture below? Is that the point of original impact? Is that -- and I'm talking about the impact detonation where the passage was. This is something from your documentation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not prepare the photo documents. My colleagues did. But as far as I can recall, this was the point of impact on the roof where the projectile struck. Now, whether this was actually caused by the projectile, itself, or just its propulsion mechanism, and whether it ricochetted, I can't really confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, what would happen and what are the conditions in which the bomb flies forward of the propulsion area -- of the propulsion element, so that the impact is caused by the propulsion element and not by the warhead?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would depend on the ballistics. I don't rule out that this is -- that this was caused by the bomb, itself, but I can also not rule out the possibility that this may have been caused by the central part, the body of the projectile, or its propulsion element.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In the transcript, you said that you did not know the ballistics of this projectile; correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know the ballistics of this particular projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. We will have to make pauses between question and answer, for the interpreter's sake, because this is very precise and we have to make sure that we are very precise and the transcript reflects that. Now, would you agree with me that in the investigation, this point was described as the original point of impact of the first ricochet?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree that this is the original point of impact, the point where the projectile hit the surface for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct - and you corrected yourself a few moments ago - that this kind of impact could not have been caused by the propulsion element, but, rather, by the warhead?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I cannot rule out either possibility, that it struck there either with its warhead or the propulsion element.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see the above photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether this is the secondary ricochet point of impact? Or, rather, tell us what this photo depicts, based on your documents.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a photo document, and we can see below that it says that this is a portion of the building of the Television of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was taken from the roof of the place where the projectile ricochetted from. And we saw a moment ago that picture. Now, I don't know exactly whether the projectile struck here and whether this was the point of the secondary ricochet or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now get the next page, 555. P1043, 555. I believe that's photo number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You did go on site, you were there; correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 552. Could we have 555, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, what do we see here? Is this the point of the second ricochet, or, rather, did the bomb fall, after this ricochet, between the Studio C and the medical office? Can you please describe this picture, this photo?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can see the description below the picture, although I have to say, again, that I was not the one who took this photo, nor did I write this caption. But it says there that the arrow shows the point on the wall where the projectile ricochetted before it fell next to the east wall of Studio C.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please pull up -- or, rather, could you please put a circle where the arrow should be, because I'm not sure that the arrow is very visible.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So what you're saying, in fact, is that this is the second ricochet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that's not my claim. I didn't say that this is a ricochet. It is possible that this is where the detonator was activated, because if this was a contact-action fuse, then it's possible -- and projectile, then it's possible that when the fuse detonated, that that's where the explosion was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And in your report, it says that the bomb ricochets from here, and there is no mention anywhere that this is where it detonated, actually?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, off the top of my head, what is in the report, but whatever is in the report is the conclusion we came to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, here on this photo, that's what it says. So would you agree with me that this caption with this photo was taken from your report, the description of the point of impact, in keeping with what the report found? Could you please read the caption under the picture?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The arrow shows the place on the wall where the projectile ricochets next to the eastern wall of Studio C."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, that's sufficient. We want to keep the same photo. Could you please now describe how it is possible that the roof of the passage bears visible marks of the point of impact, whereas there is no damage or no visible damage on the wall where the bomb fell? And I'm referring to the damage that we are talking about here, seen in this photo, where the arrow is pointing to it.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And what do you want me to compare this with?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The damage on the passage roof, the point of first impact. How do you explain this? This is almost nothing more than a scratch.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that this is a scratch. If we're talking about anything being a scratch, I would say that it was on the roof of the passage, because there were no damages on the roof of the passage, save of the pebble surface and the bitumen or tar insulation, and those were the only damages. So the concrete plate did not suffer any damage, as far as I can remember. And I apologise. I would say if we want to characterise something as a scratch, that would be on the roof, on the flat roof of the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And do you think that this is a bigger damage? We can see that the facade is damaged. Do you think that this would tally with the second point of impact of this projectile? Is this something to be expected? Can this be accounted for and explained?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that this may be expected. Can this be accounted for? Well, the projectile did not explode here, so these are just the traces of a mechanical impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. In that case, according to your findings, what could have been the angle of descent or the descent impact of the bomb when it hit the passage roof?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the break, I told you that I didn't know. We never carried out any investigations in order to determine the impact velocity of either this particular projectile or any other, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you accept what Mr. Berko Zecevic wrote in his report, and that is that the impact velocity was between 150 to 200 metres per second, which would be anything between 540 to 720 kilometres per hour?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not wish to say anything concrete here, because I can't provide an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript and for the interpreters, I have to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The impact velocity of the bomb on the initial contact on the passage roof was between 150 and 200 metres per second, and if we calculate that in terms of hours, it would be 540 to 720 kilometres per hour. Do you accept this, and this was written in Mr. Zecevic's book?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've just told you, I don't want to provide any statements. If this was written by an expert, it should be accepted in that way. I'd rather have an expert talk about that, especially an expert who was involved in that. I can't say whether I accept things or not. I'm not an expert in ballistics. I never tried to determine any velocities, so I really can't speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Do you agree that it is information from the catalogue describing this type of projectiles?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If an expert copied that from a catalogue, I suppose so. I don't know where the expert got his information from, and that's why I would not wish to voice my opinion about something that I really am not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell us, what is the mass of a modified aerial bomb, approximately? If the bomb weighs 250 kilos, how -- together with the motor and the fuel, what's its total mass?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as I've told you already, I don't know. I can tell you approximately that this aerial bomb weighs approximately 250 kilograms. I don't know what the mass of the motor is. But it was not our task and we never investigated what the overall mass of the flying projectile was. As you can read in our reports, our objective was to determine the type of the projectiles which left the traces. Possibly the trajectory or the direction from which the projectile came, that was requested from us. I never was involved in drafting such reports. And also the angle of descent, those were the data that were requested from our department. When we came to the scene, we collected data, and some of the colleagues from my department collected information, analysed the crater, in order to establish the direction from which the projectile was fired.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And can the Court now produce -- have these documents been tendered by the Prosecution? Have they been admitted? If not, could you please mark the photos? Can you date them and initial them? Or maybe we can admit the documents as they are, because everything is on record. Whatever Mr. Suljevic told us is on record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we can identify the arrow, so we can admit it as it is. But we don't have the translation. So unless it is objected to, we'll mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. There's no objection to its admission, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is translation. Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D526, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, am I right in interpreting your materials in the following way: The bomb arrived at the passage roof. It continued its trajectory, hit the wall and ricochetted from the building, and finally fell on the ground next to Studio C; am I right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one point, it damaged the roof. Then it hit the wall, and finally it fell on the floor by Studio C.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us, what is the distance between the point of first contact on the roof of the passage and the point of the second contact on the wall of the building where the bomb hit the second time?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, okay. Can the Court please produce 1D2202, 1D2202.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is a visual image of your findings or, rather, an illustration of your findings. Could you please take a look -- I said "2202," did I not? 2 -- 1D2202. Could the document please be zoomed in for everybody's benefit. Mr. Suljevic, is this the visual image of what happened; the passage, the building Studio C, and everything?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this before. However, I can accept that this is, indeed, the illustration of all that. I don't know who the author of this drawing is. I don't know who decided on the trajectory, but I can accept that this might be the distance. I can't remember exactly, I can't be precise. But here you go, this is it. I can read?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Does this correspond with the dimensions you mentioned in your report?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that in the report that we drafted in our department -- or, rather, that I finalised, that information is missing. So it says here "according to the claims of investigative organs." I don't know. When we were there, we didn't measure the distance, we didn't measure that. When I was there, we didn't measure the distance. I don't know if the technician who took the photos actually measured the distance. I don't know. However, if there's somebody that claims that that is the distance, I cannot not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I please ask you to state, for the record, the type of -- the place of ricochet, the trajectory, the place of secondary ricochet, the place of explosion? We want to be sure that we have properly identified the visual appearance of the trajectory of this projectile.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the author of this drawing is. I don't know whether this is credible, whether this is a credible reflection of the trajectory of this modified air-bomb. I don't know whether this is an angle that the projectile assumed when it hit the roof on the passage. But it is true that there was damage on the roof. There was an impact on the vertical wall, and where you see the word "Visespratnica," that's a building with several floors, and that's also a part of the television building, and this is also the place on the floor where the projectile finally exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put the date, and could you please initial this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
